title: Alertmanager pods stuck in CrashLoopBackOff, ETL job alerts failing
description: The reporting‑etl service is not receiving alert notifications. Running `kubectl get pod -l app=alertmanager` shows alertmanager-main-0 CrashLoopBackOff with 37107 restarts. The pod logs contain the line `fatal error: memory allocation failed`.
root_cause: The alertmanager container exceeded its memory limit, causing OOM kills.
resolution:
Edited the deployment to increase the memory request and limit from 200Mi to 512Mi, applied the changes, and waited for the pods to roll out:

```
kubectl set resources deployment/alertmanager --requests=memory=512Mi --limits=memory=512Mi
```

After a few minutes the pods returned to Running and alerts started flowing again.

title: Duplicate payments alerts due to alertmanager crash loops
description: Payments‑service alerts are being sent twice or not at all. `kubectl describe pod alertmanager-main-0` shows CrashLoopBackOff and the last log line: `panic: runtime error: index out of range`. The events indicate `Failed to parse config file: invalid syntax`.
root_cause: A recent config change introduced a syntax error in alertmanager.yml, causing the process to crash.
resolution:
Reverted alertmanager.yml to the previous stable version, applied the config with `kubectl apply -f alertmanager-config.yaml`, and restarted the pods:

```
kubectl rollout restart deployment/alertmanager
```

The pods stabilized and alerts were delivered correctly.

title: Alertmanager pods disappeared, user-auth API failing
description: After the AlertmanagerClusterDown alert fired, `kubectl get pods -n monitoring` showed all Alertmanager replicas in CrashLoopBackOff. The pod logs contained: `panic: failed to load config: yaml: line 12: found character that cannot start any token`. User‑auth requests were timing out because the alerting layer was unavailable.
root_cause: A recent ConfigMap update introduced a YAML syntax error, causing all Alertmanager pods to crash on startup.
resolution: I edited the `alertmanager-config` ConfigMap to fix the indentation, applied it with `kubectl apply -f alertmanager-config.yaml`, and then restarted the pods with `kubectl rollout restart deployment/alertmanager -n monitoring`. The cluster returned to healthy state and user‑auth traffic resumed.

title: Alertmanager cannot reach Kubernetes API, checkout-api stuck
description: The logs from the Alertmanager pods read: `Alertmanager: unable to connect to Kubernetes API: Get https://kubernetes.default.svc:443/api/v1/nodes: dial tcp: lookup kubernetes.default.svc on 10.0.0.0:53: no such host`. Consequently, `kubectl get events` showed many `Pending` Alertmanager pods and checkout‑api requests were delayed by missing alert notifications.
root_cause: The service account token used by Alertmanager had been rotated, but the associated secret was not updated, leaving the pods unable to authenticate to the API.
resolution: I recreated the secret for the Alertmanager service account, updated the deployment to reference the new secret, and performed `kubectl rollout restart deployment/alertmanager -n monitoring`. After verifying `kubectl describe pod` showed a healthy status, checkout‑api traffic returned to normal.

title: Search API Slack alerts stuck after upgrade
description: After the v2.3 rollout, Search API alerts stopped posting to Slack. The logs contain: `alertmanager: failed to send alert to Slack: HTTP 403: Forbidden`. `kubectl get pods -n monitoring | grep alertmanager` shows all pods healthy.
root_cause: The Slack webhook secret was rotated, but the ConfigMap used by Alertmanager was not updated, causing authentication failures.
resolution: Updated the `alertmanager-config` ConfigMap with the new Slack webhook token, then restarted the Alertmanager pods: `kubectl rollout restart deployment/alertmanager -n monitoring`. Verified the change by executing `kubectl exec alertmanager-0 -n monitoring -- cat /etc/alertmanager/config.yaml | grep slack` and confirmed alerts now appear in Slack.

title: Inventory DB alerts not reaching PagerDuty
description: Inventory DB cluster alerts are not arriving at PagerDuty. Log shows: `alertmanager: failed to send alert to PagerDuty: dial tcp 192.168.10.5:443: i/o timeout`. `kubectl describe svc pagerduty-integration` shows ClusterIP 10.96.0.42.
root_cause: A VPC firewall rule blocked outbound HTTPS traffic from the alertmanager namespace, preventing connectivity to PagerDuty.
resolution: Added an outbound rule to allow TCP port 443 to PagerDuty’s IP range, applied the new firewall config, and restarted Alertmanager pods: `kubectl rollout restart deployment/alertmanager -n monitoring`. Confirmed connectivity with `kubectl exec alertmanager-1 -n monitoring -- curl -v https://events.pagerduty.com/v2/enqueue`. Alerts are now delivered to PagerDuty.

title: Alertmanager alerts misrouted to wrong webhook
description: After the nightly deploy, PagerDuty alerts stopped firing. I saw in the logs: `level=error msg="Failed to send alert to webhook: HTTP 502 Bad Gateway"`. Running `kubectl get secret alertmanager-config -o yaml | grep data` revealed two different base64‑encoded values across the cluster.
root_cause: The alertmanager config secret was duplicated with differing content, so each pod loaded a different configuration.
resolution: Deleted the stale secret with `kubectl delete secret alertmanager-config` and redeployed the correct one from the CI pipeline using `kubectl apply -f alertmanager-config.yaml`. Then restarted the pods with `kubectl rollout restart deployment/alertmanager`. Verified consistency with `kubectl get secret alertmanager-config -o yaml | grep data` on all nodes.

title: Reporting ETL alerts suppressed due to config drift
description: The reporting‑etl jobs were failing but no alerts appeared. A log entry read: `alertmanager: config error: route 'default' not found`. Checking a pod with `kubectl exec -it alertmanager-0 -- cat /etc/alertmanager/alertmanager.yml` showed an older route configuration compared to other pods.
root_cause: A failed secret update left one alertmanager instance with an outdated alertmanager.yml, causing the config mismatch.
resolution: Re‑created the ConfigMap from the latest repository commit and applied it with `kubectl apply -f alertmanager-config.yaml`. Restarted all alertmanager pods using `kubectl rollout restart deployment/alertmanager`. Confirmed all instances now load the same YAML by inspecting the file on each pod.

title: Alertmanager config reload failing, notification worker alerts stuck
description: The notification-worker service is missing alerts because the alertmanager failed to reload. I saw this in the config‑reloader logs: `level=error ts=2021-09-24T11:24:52.69629226Z caller=runutil.go:101 msg="function failed. Retrying in next tick" err="trigger reload: reload request failed: Post "http://localhost:9093/alertmanager/-/reload": dial tcp [::1]:9093: connect: connection refused"`. The alerts never reached the notifications-worker.
root_cause: The alertmanager pod’s readiness probe was misconfigured, preventing the container from listening on port 9093 and causing the config‑reloader to time out.
resolution: I updated the alertmanager statefulset to expose port 9093 in the readiness probe, then executed `kubectl rollout restart statefulset/alertmanager-main -n monitoring` to restart the pods. After the pods came back up, I ran `amtool check-config /etc/alertmanager/config/alertmanager.yaml` to confirm the file was valid, and the alerts started propagating again.

title: Auth service monitoring alerts stopped after config reload error
description: The user-auth service stopped generating alerts after a configuration change. The config‑reloader logs contained: `trigger reload: reload request failed: Post "http://localhost:9093/alertmanager/-/reload": dial tcp [::1]:9093: connect: connection refused`. As a result, authentication failure alerts were silent.
root_cause: The alertmanager configuration file referenced a wrong host (`http://localhost`) in the reload endpoint, which was blocked by the node’s firewall, causing connection refusals.
resolution: I edited `/etc/alertmanager/config/alertmanager.yaml` to use the correct internal service address (`http://alertmanager-main:9093`) and applied the change with `kubectl apply -f alertmanager-config.yaml -n monitoring`. Then I restarted the config‑reloader container with `kubectl delete pod -l app=alertmanager-config-reloader -n monitoring` and verified the reload succeeded using `kubectl logs -c config-reloader sts/alertmanager-main -n monitoring`. Alerts for the user‑auth service resumed.

title: Alertmanager pod stuck sending PagerDuty alerts
description: The main alertmanager pod is not routing alerts to PagerDuty; Prometheus shows >50 failed notifications in the last 5 minutes. Log snippet: "Failed to send notification: timeout while connecting to pagerduty.com:443". `kubectl -n monitoring-stack logs -l 'alertmanager=main' -c alertmanager | grep -i timeout` confirms the timeout errors.
root_cause: Outbound traffic to pagerduty.com:443 was blocked by an updated firewall rule on the node hosting the alertmanager pod.
resolution: Added an iptables rule to allow outbound HTTPS to pagerduty.com: `iptables -I OUTPUT -p tcp --dport 443 -d pagerduty.com -j ACCEPT`. Then restarted the alertmanager pod with `kubectl rollout restart deployment/alertmanager -n monitoring-stack`. The alerts are now routed correctly.

title: Slack notifications for inventory-db alerts missing token
description: Slack integration for inventory-db alerts failed with 403 errors. Log snippet: "Failed to send notification: 403 Forbidden: missing token". Running `kubectl -n monitoring-stack logs -l 'alertmanager=main' -c alertmanager | grep slack` shows the 403 responses and empty webhook URL.
root_cause: The Slack webhook secret was mistakenly rotated, resulting in an empty value for the integration token.
resolution: Recreated the secret with the correct webhook URL: `kubectl create secret generic slack-webhook --from-literal=url='https://hooks.slack.com/services/ABC/DEF/GHI' -n monitoring-stack`. Then performed a rolling restart of the alertmanager deployment: `kubectl rollout restart deployment/alertmanager -n monitoring-stack`. Slack notifications resumed.

title: Alertmanager cluster reports missing member IPs
description: While reviewing the alert logs, I saw an error: "Failed to reach cluster member: no endpoints found for alertmanager-main". The service endpoints list shows 10.128.2.3,10.129.2.5,10.131.0.44 but the pods are at 10.129.2.6,10.131.0.44,10.128.2.3. One pod IP is not matching the service endpoint, causing alerts to drop.
root_cause: An outdated Endpoint entry (10.129.2.5) was left in the Service after a pod restart to a new IP (10.129.2.6).
resolution: Deleted the stale Endpoint manually: kubectl patch svc alertmanager-main -p '{"spec":{"clusterIP":"None"}}' and then recreated the Service, which regenerated the correct Endpoints. Confirmed with kubectl describe svc and the pod IPs now match.

title: Payments-service alerts not firing due to Alertmanager member mismatch
description: The payments-service health checks were stuck in a degraded state and the Alertmanager console showed "Cluster member not found". kubectl get endpoints alertmanager-main returned only two IPs while the pods report three different addresses. Logs from the alertmanager pod included "discovered endpoint 10.129.2.5 does not match any pod".
root_cause: The Service had a mis‑configured Endpoint pointing to a non‑existent pod IP (10.129.2.5), causing the cluster to think a member was missing.
resolution: Removed the incorrect Endpoint entry with kubectl delete endpoints alertmanager-main and let the Service automatically recreate the correct set of Endpoints. Verified that the payments-service alerts now propagate correctly.

title: etcd cluster stuck – no pod creations, high disk usage
description: While scaling user‑auth pods we saw "No space left on device" errors in etcd logs and kube-apiserver returned "etcd server unavailable". `kubectl get pods -n kube-etcd` shows all etcd pods are running but API calls time out. The etcd metrics dashboard shows 98% disk usage.
root_cause: The etcd data directory exceeded its quota due to a large number of old key‑value entries from deprecated feature flags.
resolution: Logged into the first etcd pod: `kubectl rsh -n kube-etcd $(kubectl get po -l app=etcd -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')`. Ran `etcdctl defrag` which freed ~1.2 GB. Updated the etcd configuration to increase `quota-backend-bytes` to 10 GB and restarted the etcd pods. Verified that new writes succeed and metrics now show 45% usage.

title: Monitoring‑stack metrics endpoint down, etcd disk full
description: Prometheus scrape failed with "etcd: connection refused" and the service‑monitoring stack reported many 5xx errors. `kubectl describe svc monitoring-stack` shows the pod status as CrashLoopBackOff, and logs contain "Failed to query etcd: space quota exceeded".
root_cause: An automated backup script had left orphaned etcd snapshots, bloating the etcd backend beyond its configured quota.
resolution: Deleted old snapshots from the etcd data directory: `rm -rf /var/lib/etcd/snap*`. Ran `etcdctl endpoint status -w table` to confirm size reduction. Restarted the monitoring‑stack pod. Updated the backup script to rotate snapshots and added a pre‑delete check for quota limits.

title: Etcd gRPC latency spike blocking order-service writes
description: Order-service pods started reporting timeouts on write operations: "rpc error: code = Unavailable desc = etcd: request timed out". Logs show increasing latency in grpc_server_handling_seconds. Kubectl logs order-service-xx show repeated "etcd: timeout" errors.
root_cause: Fragmented etcd WAL on the underlying PV caused fsync latency to exceed 10 ms, pushing the 99th‑percentile gRPC latency over the threshold.
resolution: Shrunk the etcd data directory and performed a clean compaction: ran `etcdctl compact $(etcdctl endpoint status --write-out=table | awk 'NR>1{print $2}')` on each member. After the compaction and a pod restart, WAL sync times dropped below 10 ms and latency returned to normal.

title: reporting-etl stuck due to slow etcd gRPC calls
description: The reporting ETL pipeline started stalling, with logs showing "Failed to get lease: context deadline exceeded". `kubectl describe pod reporting-etl-abc` indicated high CPU usage on the etcd node and `etcd_disk_wal_fsync_duration_seconds_bucket` spikes.
root_cause: CPU contention on the etcd control plane node caused disk fsync operations to slow down, raising gRPC request latency.
resolution: Reduced CPU limits for the etcd pods to 500m and added a dedicated CPU share; restarted the etcd cluster. Monitored the metrics and confirmed fsync times returned below 10 ms, after which the ETL pipeline resumed normal throughput.

title: etcd leader stuck, writes hanging on inventory-db
description: The inventory-db pod started returning 504 Gateway Timeout for create requests and the logs show `etcd: rpc error: code = DeadlineExceeded desc = context deadline exceeded` after a few seconds. `kubectl get pods -n inventory-db` shows the etcd container is still Running but the pod’s latency metrics spiked.
root_cause: The etcd WAL disk was experiencing high fsync latency due to a fragmented file system on the underlying block device.
resolution: Ran `umount /var/lib/etcd` and performed a filesystem defragmentation with `e2fsck -f /dev/sdb1` followed by a reboot of the node. After remounting, etcd’s fsync metrics returned to normal and the inventory-db service stabilized.

title: monitoring-stack's alerting stuck, slow responses
description: Prometheus alerts were firing at a higher frequency but the alertmanager UI was not updating; a curl to the alertmanager endpoint returned `Connection reset by peer`. The logs contain `etcd: failed to sync state: timeout while waiting for response`.
root_cause: The monitoring-stack’s etcd cluster was hitting high fsync durations caused by an SSD controller firmware issue that introduced 200ms latency spikes.
resolution: Updated the SSD firmware to the latest revision and restarted the etcd pods. Verified that the fsync duration metrics dropped below the threshold and alertmanager now processes alerts normally.

title: Etcd gRPC errors causing checkout API timeouts
description: The checkout-api was returning 504 Gateway Timeout for most POST /checkout requests. In the logs I saw: `level=error msg="grpc request failed" method=Put key=orders/1234 code=Unavailable` and `kube-system/etcd-0: rpc error: code = Unavailable desc = connection failed`.
root_cause: A transient network partition between the etcd pod and the OpenShift API server caused gRPC `Unavailable` errors.
resolution: I re‑joined the etcd cluster by restarting the etcd pod with `kubectl rollout restart deployment/etcd -n kube-etcd` and cleared the network policy that was blocking the pod on port 2379. After 2 minutes the 504 responses disappeared and the alert was cleared.

title: Order service experiencing high etcd failure rate
description: The order-service started failing to read order records, returning `Internal Server Error` to users. The pod logs contained `grpc: received unknown error: rpc error: code = ResourceExhausted desc = too many concurrent requests` and `kube-etcd/etcd-1: grpc: rpc error: code = Unavailable desc = connection refused`.
root_cause: The etcd cluster had reached its connection limit due to a misconfigured `max-txn-size` value, exhausting the gRPC quota.
resolution: I updated the etcd deployment to increase `max-txn-size` to 256KB via `kubectl edit deployment etcd -n kube-etcd` and then performed a rolling restart with `kubectl rollout restart deployment/etcd -n kube-etcd`. The order-service regained normal operation and the alert was silenced.

title: K8s API Read‑Only After Control‑Plane Node Loss
description: The API server returned `etcdserver: request timed out` on every `kubectl get pods` call. A quick check of the cluster nodes showed two master nodes reporting `NotReady` and the `etcd` pods were in `CrashLoopBackOff`. The logs from the first master node contained `etcd: quorum reached with 2/3 members`.
root_cause: One of the control‑plane nodes went offline, dropping the etcd quorum below the required majority.
resolution: Re‑started the failed master node and restored network connectivity. Then executed `kubectl get nodes -l node-role.kubernetes.io/master=` to confirm all masters were `Ready`. After the node came back online, `etcd` regained quorum and the API server returned to normal operation.

title: Reporting‑ETL Fails with Etcd Quorum Error
description: The reporting‑etl job failed with `Failed to connect to etcd: not enough members to form quorum`. `kubectl describe pod reporting-etl-xyz` showed the pod stuck in `ContainerCreating` due to a `FailedCreate` event. The etcd pod logs displayed `etcd: unable to reach quorum`.
root_cause: A network partition between two etcd pods caused the cluster to lose its majority, preventing new members from joining during pod creation.
resolution: Identified and fixed the misconfigured firewall rule that blocked TCP port 2380 between the two etcd instances. Then performed `kubectl delete pod -n openshift-etcd etcd-pod-2` to force a restart of the affected etcd pod. After the pod restarted, etcd re‑established quorum and the reporting‑etl pod started successfully.

title: Master node reboot causing etcd outage
description: All inventory-db pods are stuck in CrashLoopBackOff and `kubectl get pods -A | grep inventory-db` shows status CrashLoopBackOff. Logs from the master node show `etcd member <id> is down`. The cluster health command `etcdctl endpoint health` returns `unhealthy` for two members.
root_cause: A rolling reboot triggered by a machine configuration change brought two master nodes offline, dropping etcd quorum.
resolution: Reboot the affected master nodes one by one and verify `machineconfiguration.openshift.io/state` is `Working`. Once both masters are back, run `oc adm upgrade node --to-latest` to resume the upgrade, then check `etcdctl cluster-health` to confirm quorum restored.

title: web-frontend stuck due to etcd split-brain
description: The web-frontend service is returning 503 errors; `kubectl get pods -n web | grep web-frontend` shows all pods running but `curl -I http://web-frontend` returns `502 Bad Gateway`. In the logs a line appears: `etcd: failed to get cluster state: quorum not achieved`.
root_cause: An unexpected master node failure during an upgrade caused the etcd cluster to lose quorum, leading to split-brain and the API becoming unreachable.
resolution: SSH into the remaining healthy master, run `etcdctl member list` to identify the missing members, then restart the etcd service on the failed masters. After restarting, confirm `etcdctl cluster-health` shows all members healthy, and then restart the web-frontend pods with `kubectl rollout restart deployment/web-frontend`.

title: K8s API stuck, writes queued, user‑auth service hanging
description: While running the nightly batch, the user‑auth API started returning 503s and kubectl get pods was stuck in Pending. The logs showed “etcdserver: no leader” and the API server responded with “etcd cluster has no leader”. The cluster seemed read‑only and user logins were failing.
root_cause: A network partition isolated two control‑plane nodes, causing the etcd quorum to drop and leaving no leader.
resolution: Re‑enabled the network interface on the affected control‑plane node and restarted the kube‑control‑plane pods. After the node joined the cluster, etcd re‑elected a leader and the API resumed normal operation.

title: Reporting‑etl stuck at 0% with ETCD leader election errors
description: The reporting‑etl job stopped processing and the status remained at 0%. Logs from the ETCD container contained “etcdserver: no leader” and the job controller reported “cannot fetch lease information”. The cluster was otherwise healthy, but API writes were queued.
root_cause: A slow disk on one control‑plane node caused a prolonged disk sync, delaying the leader election and making etcd temporarily leaderless.
resolution: Optimised the disk I/O by adding a faster SSD to the node, then restarted the kube‑control‑plane pods. The disk sync times dropped, etcd re‑elected a leader, and the ETL job completed successfully.

title: Checkout API spamming info alerts after scaling
description: After adding the new instance of checkout-api, the dashboard started flooding with info-level alerts for every inventory check. Logs show `2026-10-13T12:07:45Z INFO inventory-check: inventory item missing`. The alertmanager console lists thousands of `severity=info` events, but no real problems are reported.
root_cause: The info-level alerts are not being inhibited because the InfoInhibitor alert is missing the necessary namespace label, so it never activates to suppress them.
resolution: Updated the InfoInhibitor alert definition to include `namespace=checkout-api` labels and redeployed the Alertmanager config. After reload, the info alerts stopped firing and the dashboard returned to normal.

title: User-auth alerts overwhelmed by info noise during login surge
description: During a login spike, the alertmanager UI shows an explosion of `info` alerts for `user-auth` like `info: login attempt succeeded`. The UI shows `severity=info` alerts but no warnings. The system is still working, but the noise makes real alerts hard to spot.
root_cause: The InfoInhibitor alert was not routed to the null receiver, so it could not inhibit the info alerts for the user-auth namespace.
resolution: Added the null receiver to the Alertmanager configuration and reconfigured the InfoInhibitor alert to route to it. Reloaded Alertmanager; info alerts are now suppressed and real alerts are visible again.

title: network interface flaps on monitoring node, ETL jobs stalling
description: The monitoring‑stack pod is repeatedly restarting due to a network error. Logs show "tcp: sendmsg: Network interface down" and the pod status is stuck in CrashLoopBackOff. kubectl get pods shows the pod is in pending state for 12 minutes.
root_cause: The NIC on the node hosting the monitoring‑stack pod was experiencing intermittent cable disconnection due to a faulty RJ45 connector.
resolution: Replaced the defective Ethernet cable and reseated the NIC in the server. Ran `kubectl delete pod <monitoring-stack-pod>` to let the deployment recreate it. Verified connectivity with `ping` and `mtr` to ensure stability.

title: search‑api connectivity lost after interface flapping
description: search‑api instances started returning "connection refused" errors. `kubectl logs` shows "dial tcp 10.0.0.5:9200: connect: network is unreachable". The service is unable to reach Elasticsearch cluster.
root_cause: A misconfigured network switch port caused the node's NIC to toggle between up and down, dropping packets to the Elasticsearch cluster.
resolution: Re‑enabled the switch port and applied a static MAC binding to prevent flapping. Updated the node's network interface configuration to use a fixed IP via DHCP reservation. Restarted the search‑api pods with `kubectl rollout restart deployment/search-api` and confirmed traffic resumed.

title: Prometheus can't reach search‑api pods
description: Prometheus logs show "cannot scrape target http://search-api:9100/metrics: connection timed out" and the /targets page marks all search‑api endpoints as DOWN. The up==0 query spikes at the same time. The web‑frontend remains responsive but we have no metrics for search‑api.
root_cause: A recently applied NetworkPolicy on the search‑api namespace only allowed egress to external services, blocking Prometheus service from reaching the pods’ metrics port.
resolution:
Applied a rule to allow ingress from the Prometheus namespace to port 9100 on search‑api pods: kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-prometheus
  namespace: search-api
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  ingress:
  - from:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          name: monitoring
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 9100
EOF
Restarted the Prometheus pod to pick up policy changes. Metrics resumed within minutes.

title: Order‑service metrics not being scraped after rollout
description: After the latest deploy of order‑service, Prometheus reports "failed to scrape http://order-service:9100/metrics: no healthy upstream" and the /targets page shows the targets in a DOWN state. The service itself is up and serving HTTP requests fine. The logs contain "Unable to fetch metrics: connection refused".
root_cause: The ServiceMonitor for order‑service was updated to use a wrong port selector; the pods expose metrics on 9110, but the ServiceMonitor still points to 9100.
resolution: Updated the ServiceMonitor resource to point to the correct port: kubectl patch servicemonitor order-service-monitor -n monitoring --type merge -p '{"spec":{"jobLabel":"order-service","targets":{"labels":{"app.kubernetes.io/name":"order-service"}},"port":"metrics"}}' and ensured the Service exposes port 9110. After applying the patch, Prometheus started scraping again within a few seconds.

title: Alertmanager down, no alerts reaching PagerDuty
description: The Alertmanager pod on the prod cluster stopped sending any alerts. I saw repeated logs like "[error] failed to push metrics to Prometheus: connection refused" and kubectl get pods -n monitoring shows the alertmanager pod in CrashLoopBackOff. No PagerDuty notifications were received.
root_cause: The Alertmanager configuration file was overwritten with an invalid TLS cert path, causing it to crash on startup.
resolution: Restored the original config by rolling back the ConfigMap, reloaded Alertmanager with `kubectl rollout restart deployment/alertmanager -n monitoring`, and verified the pod was running. Confirmed alerts are now forwarded to PagerDuty.

title: DeadMansSnitch not firing, missing watchdog signal
description: The DeadMansSnitch integration for the reporting-etl service stopped firing. The webhook endpoint returned 500 errors: "WebhookError: timeout waiting for response". The Watchdog alert was stuck in firing state with no resolution logs.
root_cause: A firewall rule was inadvertently applied to the monitoring namespace, blocking outbound traffic to the DeadMansSnitch endpoint.
resolution: Removed the restrictive egress rule with `kubectl delete networkpolicy deny-dms -n monitoring`, restarted the reporting-etl deployment, and verified the DeadMansSnitch webhook now receives pings. The Watchdog alert resolved automatically.

title: kube-state-metrics list ops failing for payments-service metrics
description: When I queried the payment service pod metrics, I got a 500 error from kube-state-metrics: "rpc error: code = Internal desc = failed to list resources: Get https://kube-state-metrics:9100/api/v1/namespaces/default/pods: TLS handshake timeout". The `kubectl get pods -A` shows the kube-state-metrics pod is healthy, but the logs contain repeated `list error` messages.
root_cause: The service account token mounted in the kube-state-metrics pod was revoked, causing authentication failures for list calls.
resolution:
Recreated the service account and secret for kube-state-metrics, updated the pod spec, and restarted the deployment:
1. `kubectl delete secret kube-state-metrics-token`
2. `kubectl create secret generic kube-state-metrics-token --from-literal=token=$(cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token)`
3. `kubectl rollout restart deployment/kube-state-metrics`

title: web-frontend metrics missing due to kube-state-metrics list errors
description: The web-frontend health check started returning 503s. `curl -sS http://kube-state-metrics:9100/metrics | grep web_frontend` returned nothing and the log showed "Error listing resources: Get https://kube-state-metrics:9100/api/v1/namespaces/default/services: network timeout".
root_cause: A new network policy was applied that blocked egress from kube-state-metrics to the API server, breaking list operations.
resolution:
Removed the restrictive egress rule from the network policy, and verified connectivity:
1. `kubectl delete networkpolicy kube-state-metrics-egress`
2. `kubectl exec -it kube-state-metrics-0 -- curl -I https://kubernetes.default.svc` returned 200 OK

title: Metrics missing for user-auth pods after recent deploy
description: The Prometheus scrape for user‑auth is timing out: `i/o timeout` when pulling `/metrics`. In the kube‑state‑metrics logs we see `shard 2: failed to connect to API server: unauthorized`. The UI shows "No data" in the Auth latency graph.
root_cause: The ServiceAccount token for shard 2 was rotated and the new token was not propagated to the kube‑state‑metrics container, causing authentication failures.
resolution: We re‑mounted the updated service account token by deleting the kube‑state‑metrics pod (`kubectl delete pod -n monitoring kube-state-metrics-2`), which caused a new pod to start with the correct token. After 2 minutes the metrics started appearing again.

title: Web‑frontend reporting ETL metrics suddenly disappear
description: Prometheus alerts triggered for "reporting‑etl CPU usage" dropping to 0. The logs of the second shard show `shard 2: failed to discover resources: no such resource: pod`. The web‑frontend health endpoint returns a 500 with "metrics unavailable".
root_cause: NetworkPolicy rules were updated to block traffic to the API server from shard 2’s namespace, preventing kube‑state‑metrics from querying pod information.
resolution: We edited the NetworkPolicy (`kubectl edit netpol -n monitoring kube-state-metrics`) to allow egress to `kubernetes.default.svc:443` from the shard 2 pod. After re‑applying the policy, the metrics resumed and the alerts cleared.

title: kube-state-metrics shards gone missing – metrics dead on checkout-api
description: The Prometheus scrape of kube-state-metrics failed with `timeout during metrics collection`. `kubectl logs kube-state-metrics-xx-yy -n monitoring` shows a stack trace: `panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference`. The dashboard for checkout-api pods shows `0` for CPU and memory metrics.
root_cause: A recent rolling update of the kube-state-metrics image replaced the `shards` binary with a version that dropped support for the `--enable-shards` flag, causing shards to stop initializing.
resolution: Rolled back the kube-state-metrics deployment to the previous image tag (`v2.4.1`). Then recreated the `kube-state-metrics` StatefulSet to re‑init shards. Verified metrics returned by querying `http://kube-state-metrics:8080/metrics` and re‑enabled `--enable-shards=true`.

title: monitoring-stack lost resource metrics after pod eviction
description: Prometheus targets for `monitoring-stack` started returning `connection refused` for `/metrics`. `kubectl get pods -n monitoring -o wide | grep Evicted` shows several pods marked as `Evicted`. The kube-state-metrics logs contain `shards missing: 3` and `shard 2 not available`.
root_cause: The node where the kube-state-metrics shards ran ran out of memory and the kubelet evicted the pods, but the pod eviction was not handled by the statefulset's `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`, leaving stale metrics endpoints.
resolution: Increased the memory limits for kube-state-metrics pods to 512Mi and updated the StatefulSet to set `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60`. Deployed a new replica to replace the evicted pod and restarted Prometheus to re‑discover the metrics. Confirmed metrics are now visible in Grafana dashboards.

title: web-frontend metrics stopped at 5xx errors
description: The dashboard stopped pulling CPU/memory stats for web-frontend; the metrics endpoint returned “400 Bad Request: watch failed: error decoding watch result”. kubectl logs kube-state-metrics-7d8f6c8b9c-xyz shows "Error from server (InternalError): watch api: internal error".
root_cause: The kube-state-metrics service account token had expired, causing watch authentication failures.
resolution: Rotated the service account token: deleted the old secret, re‑created it with `kubectl create secret generic ksm-token --from-literal=token=$(cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token)` and updated the deployment. Restarted the pod with `kubectl rollout restart deployment/kube-state-metrics`. Metrics resumed normal flow.

title: search-api metrics missing after network policy change
description: Search‑api was showing no latency metrics; logs contain "kube-state-metrics: watch failed: failed to connect to apiserver: dial tcp 10.0.0.1:443: connect: network is unreachable". kubectl get pods -n monitoring shows kube-state-metrics pod stuck in CrashLoopBackOff.
root_cause: A recent network policy update blocked traffic from kube-state-metrics to the API server, breaking watch operations.
resolution: Updated the network policy to allow egress to the API server on port 443 from the kube-state-metrics namespace: applied `kubectl apply -f ksm-allow-apiserver.yaml`. Deleted the failing pod to allow a fresh start. After 2 minutes the pod entered Running state and metrics appeared again.

title: notifications-worker pod stuck in throttled state
description:
The notifications-worker deployment started showing high CPU usage in metrics and the pod logs contain repeated "cpu throttling" warnings: 
```
2026-10-13T12:04:32Z ERROR [throttling] Process pid=3125 was throttled for 1500ms
``` 
The pod is still running but response times are 5× slower.
root_cause: The container was allocated 200m CPU request but the node’s kernel was too old to honor cgroup CPU limits, causing persistent throttling.
resolution:
Updated the node to kernel 5.10 by rebooting and applied the patch.
Then increased the container’s CPU limit to 500m:
```
kubectl patch deployment notifications-worker -p '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"notifications-worker","resources":{"limits":{"cpu":"500m"}}}]}}}'
```

title: order-service latency spike due to CPU throttling
description:
After the order-service deployment, metrics showed CPU throttling spikes. The pod logs include:
```
2026-10-13T12:07:15Z WARN [cpu] Throttled: 3.2s over 10s
``` 
Requests from the frontend timed out and the health check started failing.
root_cause: The order-service container was using the default CPU request of 100m but the pod was scheduled on a node with an outdated kernel that misallocated CPU resources.
resolution:
First upgraded the node kernel to 5.15.
Then modified the deployment to set a higher request and limit:
```
kubectl set resources deployment order-service --containers=order-service --requests=cpu=200m --limits=cpu=400m
``` 
After the changes, CPU throttling stopped and latency returned to normal.

title: web-frontend can't load metrics – API timeout error
description: The web‑frontend UI is stuck on the dashboard and shows a timeout. The console logs contain `kube-api: timeout waiting for response from aggregated API`. `kubectl get apiservices -o wide` returns `Error from server (GatewayTimeout): request timed out`. The page keeps flashing "Error loading data".
root_cause: The aggregated API server was blocked by a firewall rule that blocked outbound traffic to the kube‑api‑aggregated service on port 443.
resolution: Removed the incorrect iptables rule on the node running the aggregated API: `iptables -D OUTPUT -p tcp --dport 443 -j DROP`. Restarted the kube-apiserver pods (`kubectl rollout restart deployment/kube-apiserver`). After the restart, metrics loaded normally.

title: inventory-db scaling fails – custom metrics API unreachable
description: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler for inventory-db reports `failed to fetch custom metrics: unable to connect to aggregated API`. The HPA logs show `Get "https://kubernetes.default.svc:443/apis/custom.metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1" : net/http: request canceled while waiting for connection`. The pods stop scaling.
root_cause: A NetworkPolicy was applied that blocked traffic from the autoscaler pod namespace to the kube‑api‑aggregated namespace.
resolution: Updated the NetworkPolicy to allow egress to the aggregated API namespace: added `to: [{podSelector: {}}]` for the `custom.metrics.k8s.io` group. Applied the policy (`kubectl apply -f allow-autoscaler.yaml`) and verified HPA functioning with `kubectl get hpa inventory-db`.

title: Checkout API stuck: API server errors on every request
description: When hitting `/checkout` I get a 502 response and the logs show `kube-apiserver: error aggregating API responses`. The `kubectl get pods` command on the node returns `No resources found`. The error line in the API server log reads: `aggregated apis not available: 4 errors in the last 10m`.
root_cause: A NetworkPolicy on the control plane node inadvertently blocked the aggregated API service (`kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local`) from reaching the kube-apiserver pods.
resolution: Removed the restrictive policy from the `kube-system` namespace and added an allow rule for `kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local` on port 443. Ran `kubectl apply -f allow-k8s-api.yaml` and verified the checkout API responded normally. Restarted the kube-apiserver pods to clear any stale state.

title: User‑Auth can't read metrics; service unhealthy
description: The user-auth microservice threw a timeout when fetching Prometheus metrics: `metrics request to kube-system/prometheus: timeout`. In the node logs I saw `kube-apiserver: aggregated API error 4 times in 10m`. `kubectl get services -n kube-system` shows the Prometheus service is present but unreachable from the node.
root_cause: A firewall rule on the node had been updated to block outbound HTTPS traffic to the Prometheus pod, causing the aggregated API to fail when user-auth tried to pull custom metrics.
resolution: Re-enabled outbound HTTPS (port 443) in the node’s firewall configuration. Tested connectivity with `curl -k https://prometheus.kube-system.svc.cluster.local/metrics` and confirmed success. Restarted user-auth to re‑register metrics collection.

title: Kubernetes API unreachable – cluster hangs
description: The monitoring alert triggered and `kubectl cluster-info` returned `Unable to connect to the server: dial tcp 10.0.0.5:6443: i/o timeout`. Web‑frontend requests were timing out and order-service logs showed `GET /api/orders: connection refused`.
root_cause: All kube-apiserver pods crashed due to a sudden surge in etcd replication lag, causing them to exit with SIGKILL.
resolution: Identified and restarted the failing etcd pods: `kubectl -n kube-system delete pod etcd-0` and allowed the control plane to rebalance. After the pods were back in Ready state, `kubectl get nodes` returned healthy nodes and API access was restored.

title: Order service unable to create orders after API downtime
description: Order-service returned `500 Internal Server Error` with stack trace `kubernetes.client.rest.ApiException: 503 Service Unavailable` when attempting to list pods. The API server was inaccessible from the service pods.
root_cause: NetworkPolicy was misconfigured, blocking Prometheus pods from accessing kube-apiserver, which caused the API to time out for all non‑cluster‑internal traffic.
resolution: Updated the NetworkPolicy to allow traffic from `kube-system` namespace to `kube-system` namespace on port 6443: `kubectl apply -f allow-prometheus-to-apiserver.yaml`. After policy reload, order-service successfully communicated with the API and the error disappeared.

title: Kube API errors spiking, order-service stuck
description: The order-service pods are repeatedly failing to reconcile, showing "error: failed to create pod: Internal error occurred: the server could not find the resource" and kubectl get pods returns many pending with status "CrashLoopBackOff". The cluster API latency is over 2s for GET requests.
root_cause: A mis‑configured kube‑apiserver admission controller was rejecting a large batch of requests due to exceeding the rate limit, causing a high error rate.
resolution:
Restarted the kube-apiserver pod to reset the admission controller state:

```
kubectl -n kube-system delete pod kube-apiserver-0
```

Verified API latency returned to < 200ms and order-service pods stabilized.

title: Reporting ETL stuck in API error loop
description: The reporting-etl jobs were timing out with logs like "api error: Get https://k8s.default.svc.cluster.local/apis/apps/v1/namespaces/etl/pods: request timed out" and the ETL status shows many "Failed" events. The API server was returning 500 errors for pod queries.
root_cause: A sudden spike in the number of concurrent API calls from the ETL service exceeded the kube-apiserver's max open connections, triggering internal server errors.
resolution:
Scaled the kube-apiserver replicas from 1 to 3 and increased `--max-requests-inflight` to 5000:

```
kubectl scale deployment kube-apiserver --replicas=3 -n kube-system
kubectl edit deployment kube-apiserver -n kube-system
```

After the scale and config change, API errors dropped to 0 and ETL jobs completed.

title: API Server throttling kills checkout API
description: The checkout‑api app is returning 503 errors: "The request was rejected by the API server due to throttling". Logs show a spike in `apiserver_flowcontrol_rejected_requests_total{flow_schema="default"}`. Clients can no longer create orders.
root_cause: The default flow control schema had its qps limit lowered by a recent config change, causing 20%+ request terminations.
resolution: Reviewed the flow‑control config in `kube-system` and increased the `maxQps` for the default schema from 50 to 200. Restarted the apiserver pod to apply changes and verified metrics dropped below 5%.

title: Reporting‑ETL stuck, API throttling blocking data sync
description: Reporting‑ETL is timing out on `kubectl get pods -A` with error: `request rejected: too many concurrent requests`. The ETL process stalls and downstream dashboards show stale data.
root_cause: The `etl-flow` schema was misconfigured with a very low concurrency limit, causing the ETL to hit flow‑control throttling.
resolution: Updated `etl-flow` flow‑control config to allow 100 qps and 1000 concurrent requests, applied via `kubectl apply -f flow-control-etl.yaml`. Restarted the ETL pod and confirmed it resumes processing.

title: Payments service pods failing to auth to API
description: The payments-service pod started reporting "Failed to authenticate client: certificate expired" and kubelet logs showed "client certificate expired" errors. `kubectl get pods payments-service-xxxxx -o wide` returned Pending status. The pod logs contain "x509: certificate has expired".
root_cause: The client certificate for the payments-service service account expired 3 days ago.
resolution: Regenerated the service account token and updated the kubeconfig in the payments-service deployment. Applied `kubectl delete pod payments-service-xxxxx` to force a restart, ensuring the new token is used. Verified with `kubectl describe pod payments-service-xxxxx` that the status changed to Running.

title: Web‑frontend unable to fetch API data
description: Users reported 503 errors when accessing the web‑frontend. The frontend logs show "GET /api/... 502: Bad Gateway" and the Kubernetes event stream contains "kubelet: client certificate expired" for the web-frontend pod. `kubectl logs web-frontend-abcde` shows "x509: certificate has expired".
root_cause: The web‑frontend pod’s in‑cluster client certificate had reached its 7‑day warning threshold and was considered expired by the API server.
resolution: Recreated the web‑frontend pod by running `kubectl delete pod web-frontend-abcde`. The new pod automatically picked up a fresh client certificate from the service account. Confirmed connectivity with `curl -k https://kubernetes.default.svc` from inside the pod and the 502 errors disappeared.

title: checkout-api API server errors spike after recent deploy
description: Since the latest canary release, the checkout‑api logs are throwing a 502 error: "Failed to get resource: Get "https://k8s-api:6443/api/v1/namespaces/default/pods?limit=500": timeout". The Kubernetes client is returning "client-go: request rate exceeded" in the metrics. The API calls from the service are timing out and the dashboard shows a 1.4% error rate over the past 15 minutes.
root_cause: The new client library in checkout-api was compiled with an older version of client-go that does not support the updated API server rate limits, causing excessive retries and timeouts.
resolution: Rolled back checkout-api to the previous image tag that used client-go v0.22. Updated the deployment with "kubectl rollout undo deployment/checkout-api" and verified that the error rate dropped below 0.2%. Monitored the service for the next 30 minutes to ensure stability.

title: inventory-db experiencing API client errors after scaling event
description: inventory-db logs show "kubernetes.client: unexpected status code 429" and the pod is stuck in a retry loop. The service is reporting "Failed to list pods: too many requests" and the Prometheus alert shows a 1.5% error rate. The kubectl get pods command on the node shows "client-go: request rate exceeded" messages.
root_cause: During the node pool resize, inventory-db's CPU limits were set too low (100m) causing the client to be throttled by the API server.
resolution: Increased the CPU request/limit for inventory-db to 250m/500m using "kubectl set resources deployment/inventory-db --requests=cpu=250m --limits=cpu=500m". Restarted the deployment and confirmed that the error rate fell below 0.1% within 10 minutes.

title: inventory-db pod stuck in Waiting – no config mounted
description: The inventory-db pod keeps reporting "ContainerCreating" in the status. `kubectl -n prod describe pod inventory-db-abc123` shows an event: *Warning FailedMount 3s (x3 over 1m) Unable to mount volume "config-volume".* The logs never start. This is blocking API requests to the inventory service.
root_cause: The ConfigMap volume for inventory-db was deleted; the pod still references it.
resolution: Recreated the missing ConfigMap `inventory-config` and redeployed the pod. After running `kubectl delete pod inventory-db-abc123` and letting the deployment recreate it, the pod moved to Running and logs streamed normally.

title: reporting-etl worker hanging in Waiting due to missing secret
description: The reporting-etl worker pod is in a Waiting state and the logs show `Error: secret "etl-creds" not found`. The pod description shows an event: *FailedMount 5s (x2 over 2m) Secret "etl-creds" not found*; the API server reports no events after that.
root_cause: The secret `etl-creds` was inadvertently deleted from the namespace.
resolution: Created the secret again with `kubectl create secret generic etl-creds --from-file=key=secret.key -n prod` and restarted the worker deployment (`kubectl rollout restart deployment/reporting-etl`). The pod transitioned to Running and processed the ETL jobs.

title: KubeControllerManager vanished – cluster stuck, no pods spinning
description: Since 13:02 UTC the payments-service API calls are timing out and kubectl get pods returns no running pods. The logs show `panic: unable to find kube-controller-manager target in prometheus` and the cluster nodes are reporting `kube-controller-manager: not found` on `/etc/systemd/system`.
root_cause: The kube-controller-manager pod was evicted due to insufficient node memory and never restarted because the deployment had a misconfigured resource request.
resolution: I patched the deployment to increase the memory request to 2Gi, then ran `kubectl rollout restart deployment kube-controller-manager -n kube-system` to trigger a fresh start. After 5 minutes the pod was back online and the cluster began reconciling resources again.

title: Notifications worker stalls after controller manager crash
description: The notifications-worker kept failing with `Error from server (NotFound): pods "controller-manager" not found`. The service logs showed repeated `kube-controller-manager down` errors and the worker could not create required CRDs.
root_cause: The kube-controller-manager crash caused the custom resource definitions to become unreachable, leading the worker to error out when trying to reconcile its own resources.
resolution: I manually deleted the stale controller-manager pod and re‑deployed it with `kubectl delete pod kube-controller-manager-0 -n kube-system && kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/master/cluster/addons/kube-controller-manager.yaml`. Once the pod was running, the worker resumed normal operation and CRDs were reconciled.

title: Pods stuck in Pending after node failure – CPU limits too high
description: After the recent node drain for maintenance, several of our ETL pods are now stuck in Pending with the message "Unable to schedule pod "reporting-etl-processor-xyz" on any node". `kubectl get pods -A | grep reporting-etl | grep Pending` shows all instances pending. The cluster reports 98% CPU usage but still cannot schedule new pods.
root_cause: CPU requests for the reporting‑etl pods were set to 4 cores each, exceeding the cluster's available capacity and causing an overcommit when a node went down.
resolution: Reduced the CPU request for reporting‑etl to 2 cores via `kubectl patch deployment reporting-etl -p '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"etl","resources":{"requests":{"cpu":"2"}}}]}}}'`. Then added a small node pool with 8x4vCPU nodes to absorb the load (`eksctl create nodegroup --node-type t3.medium --nodes 4`). After scaling, all pods rescheduled successfully.

title: Monitoring stack pods pending after node failure – need immediate fix
description: The monitoring‑stack pods are in Pending state since the last node reboot. `kubectl describe pod kube-state-metrics-abc | grep 'Failed to schedule'` shows "Failed to schedule pod due to insufficient CPU resources". Metrics are not being scraped and alerting is silent.
root_cause: The monitoring‑stack containers requested 1.5 CPU each, while the cluster only had 1 CPU available per node, leading to an overcommit condition when a node failed.
resolution: Scaled down the CPU request to 1 core per container using `kubectl set resources deployment kube-state-metrics --requests=cpu=1`. Deployed an additional node pool with 10x2vCPU nodes (`eksctl create nodegroup --node-type t3.small --nodes 10`). After the new nodes joined, all monitoring pods were scheduled and metrics resumed.

title: Pods stuck in Pending after node drain
description: After a scheduled maintenance, several payment-service pods remained in Pending state. `kubectl get pods -n payments-service` showed `0/3` ready and the logs contain `FailedScheduling:0: exceeded CPU request for namespace payments-service`
root_cause: CPU requests for the payments-service namespace were overcommitted, exceeding the cluster’s available CPU capacity.
resolution: Reduced the CPU request for payments-service by 30%, added a small node pool with t3.medium instances, and updated the deployment to use pod priority 2000. Re‑scheduled the pods with `kubectl delete pod <pod-name>` and verified they became Running.

title: Notifications-worker throttled due to CPU quota overcommit
description: The notifications-worker started throwing `kubelet: CPU request exceeded` errors and the queue latency spiked. `kubectl describe nodes | grep -i allocatable` showed a sudden drop in allocatable CPU across nodes.
root_cause: The namespace notifications-worker had a CPU quota that exceeded the cluster’s total CPU, causing the scheduler to reject new pods.
resolution: Adjusted the namespace quota to match actual usage, scaled up the node pool by 2 x m5.large nodes, and applied a pod priority class to keep critical notifications from being preempted. Confirmed that pods are now running and latency returned to normal.

title: Inventory‑DB DaemonSet pods leaking on worker nodes
description: The inventory‑db daemonset pods are running on three worker nodes that should not host them. `kubectl get pods -n inventory-db -l app=inventory-daemon -o wide` shows them on nodes marked with `worker=true, gpu=true`. The pod logs contain: `Failed to schedule: PodAffinity: No nodes satisfy pod affinity`
root_cause: A nodeSelector in the daemonset template incorrectly referenced `gpu=true`, causing the scheduler to place pods on GPU nodes even though they should run only on `worker=true` nodes
resolution: Updated the daemonset to use `nodeSelector: { worker: "true" }` and removed the `gpu=true` selector. Applied the change with `kubectl apply -f inventory-daemonset.yaml` and manually deleted the mis‑scheduled pods to trigger rescheduling.

title: Reporting‑ETL worker pods stuck due to node taint mis‑match
description: The reporting‑etl worker daemonset has 4 pods in `Pending` state. `kubectl describe pod <pod>` shows `Error: pod affinity and anti‑affinity rules conflict with node taints`. Log snippet: `Node <node> taint {dedicated=analytics:NoSchedule} is preventing pod scheduling`
root_cause: The node pool was tainted with `dedicated=analytics:NoSchedule`, but the daemonset did not include the matching toleration, so the scheduler evicted the pods.
resolution: Added a toleration to the daemonset spec: `tolerations: - key: dedicated - value: analytics - effect: NoSchedule`. Applied with `kubectl apply -f reporting-etl-daemonset.yaml` and recreated the pods. All pods are now scheduled correctly.

title: Daemonset pods stuck in Pending on web-frontend nodes
description:
The web‑frontend DaemonSet has 3 pods showing 'Pending' in `kubectl get pods -n web-frontend`. The logs contain: `Failed to schedule pod: no nodes available that match node affinity`.

The pods are not starting, causing intermittent page loads.
root_cause: Node affinity rules were too restrictive, only allowing pods on nodes labeled `role=frontend` which were already at capacity.
resolution: Removed the `nodeAffinity` requirement from the DaemonSet template, re‑applied the manifest, and verified pods transitioned to Running. Confirmed that all frontend nodes have sufficient resources.

title: monitoring‑stack kubelet stuck scheduling Prometheus pods
description:
Prometheus pods under monitoring‑stack are in `ContainerCreating` with the error: `Failed to create pod sandbox: error creating kubelet sandbox container: failed to create pod sandbox: OCI runtime create failed`.

`kubectl describe pod prometheus-0 -n monitoring-stack` shows `PodSchedulingError: Failed to schedule pod: no nodes available that match node taints`.
root_cause: The monitoring‑stack DaemonSet had a taint tolerance for `node-role.kubernetes.io/monitoring:NoSchedule` but nodes were labeled with `monitoring=true` and the DaemonSet lacked the matching toleration.
resolution:
Updated the DaemonSet to include `tolerations:
  - key: "node-role.kubernetes.io/monitoring"
    operator: Exists
    effect: NoSchedule` and redeployed. All pods now schedule correctly.

title: user-auth DaemonSet stuck: pods stuck in Terminating
description:
The user‑auth daemonset pods keep showing as 'Terminating' in the cluster. `kubectl -n auth get pods -l app=user-auth-daemon` returns:
```
NAME                                  READY   STATUS      RESTARTS   AGE
user-auth-daemon-7d9f5c7c-abcde   0/1     Terminating   0          12m
``` 
The logs show `Error: failed to delete pod: timeout waiting for pod to be deleted.`
root_cause: The pod had a long termination grace period (180s) and the node was drained, causing the pod to never finish shutting down.
resolution: Reduced the termination grace period to 30s in the DaemonSet spec, restarted the DaemonSet with `kubectl rollout restart daemonset user-auth-daemon -n auth`, and waited for pods to finish terminating. All pods are now running normally.

title: monitoring‑stack DaemonSet rollout blocked by node affinity
description:
The prometheus node exporter DaemonSet fails to roll out. `kubectl describe daemonset prometheus-node-exporter -n monitoring` shows:
```
Desired: 3
Current: 3
Ready: 3
Available: 3
``` 
but `kubectl get pods -n monitoring -l app=prometheus-node-exporter` lists pods in `Pending` with events:
```
FailedScheduling  3s  default-scheduler  0/3 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient cpu.
```
root_cause: A recent image update added GPU resource requests, but only two nodes have GPUs, so the DaemonSet could not schedule the third pod.
resolution: Removed the GPU request from the DaemonSet pod template, applied the change with `kubectl apply -f prometheus-node-exporter.yaml -n monitoring`, and the pending pods scheduled successfully.

title: Deployment stuck in 0 ready replicas after recent rollout
description: After deploying the latest patch to monitoring-stack, the deployment status shows "Replicas: 0/3" and the pods are all in CrashLoopBackOff. `kubectl get pods -n monitoring-stack` shows: `myapp-5d6c7b7f9b-abcde   CrashLoopBackOff   2/1   1d`. The deployment history shows the new ReplicaSet was created but never scheduled.
root_cause: The new pod template requested GPU resources that were not available on any node, causing scheduling failures.
resolution: Updated the deployment manifest to remove the GPU request and re‑deployed: `kubectl -n monitoring-stack set image deployment/monitoring-stack myapp=repo:tag`. Verified that pods are now scheduled and running with `kubectl get pods -n monitoring-stack`. Monitored the rollout status until "successfully rolled out".

title: Checkout API rollout failing due to missing CPU limits
description: Checkout‑API deployment went from 3 ready pods to 0 after a new release. `kubectl describe deployment checkout-api -n services` shows: `Failed to create pod: failed to schedule pod: insufficient CPU resources`. The HPA was not triggered and new ReplicaSet pods were pending.
root_cause: The new container image omitted the CPU limit, causing the scheduler to reject pods because of cluster resource pressure.
resolution: Added CPU limits to the deployment spec (`spec.template.spec.containers[0].resources.limits.cpu: 500m`) and applied the change: `kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml -n services`. Then performed a forced rollout restart: `kubectl rollout restart deployment/checkout-api -n services`. All pods returned to ready state and traffic restored.

title: Web-frontend pods stuck at 1/3 replicas
description: The web‑frontend service is showing only 1 running pod while the deployment expects 3. `kubectl get pods -n web -l app=web-frontend -o wide` shows the other two pods in Pending state with reason "Unschedulable". Logs from kubelet show "Failed to schedule pod due to node affinity".
root_cause: Pod affinity rules required the pods to run on nodes labeled with gpu=true, but the new nodes added by autoscaler did not have the GPU label, causing scheduling failures.
resolution: Updated the deployment spec to remove the gpu=true node affinity, applied the change with `kubectl apply -f web-frontend-deploy.yaml`, and verified all replicas were running with `kubectl get deployment web-frontend -n web`. No further action needed.

title: Checkout‑API replicas reduced after HPA misconfiguration
description: Checkout‑API was scaling down to 1 replica from the desired 4. The HPA status shows `Desired: 4, Current: 1, Age: 5m`. The HPA controller logs contain "Failed to scale deployment due to insufficient CPU requests".
root_cause: The CPU request values in the deployment were set to 0, causing the HPA to consider the current CPU usage as 0 and not trigger scaling.
resolution: Set realistic CPU request values in the deployment (`resources.requests.cpu: 250m`) and redeployed with `kubectl apply -f checkout-api-deploy.yaml`. The HPA immediately scaled to 4 replicas, confirmed by `kubectl get hpa checkout-api -n checkout`.

title: HPA maxed out on monitoring‑stack, no new pods being created
description: The monitoring‑stack deployment is stuck at 5 replicas for the past 20 minutes. `kubectl get hpa monitoring-stack -o yaml | grep desired` shows desired replicas 5 while max replicas is 5. Logs from the pod show "HorizontalPodAutoscaler failed to update target: reached maximum replica count".
root_cause: The HPA was configured with a max replicas value of 5, which is lower than the required scaling threshold during peak load.
resolution: Updated the HPA manifest to set `maxReplicas: 10` and applied the change with `kubectl apply -f monitoring-stack-hpa.yaml`. Verified scaling with `kubectl get hpa monitoring-stack -w`. No further scaling issues observed.

title: search‑api HPA stuck at limit, causing request timeouts
description: search‑api is experiencing 504 Gateway Timeout errors. `kubectl describe hpa search-api` shows desired replicas 15 but current replicas 15, max 15. The metrics server reports CPU usage at 95% for all pods.
root_cause: The HPA CPU target was set too high (80%) relative to the actual load, and the max replicas was set to 15, which is insufficient during traffic spikes.
resolution: Reduced the CPU target to 50% in the HPA definition and increased `maxReplicas` to 30. Applied changes with `kubectl apply -f search-api-hpa.yaml` and confirmed new scaling behavior with `kubectl get hpa search-api -w`. The timeouts have ceased.

title: User‑auth pods stuck at 2 replicas, HPA not kicking in
description: The user‑auth service kept running only 2 pods while the desired count was 8. `kubectl get hpa user-auth-hpa -o jsonpath='{.status.currentReplicas}/{.status.desiredReplicas}'` returned `2/8` and logs showed `HorizontalPodAutoscaler: scaling from 2 to 8 pods` but no pods appeared. The cluster was full of pending pods. Error line: `Error: failed to find node for pod "user-auth-5d4c6b7f-xxxx"`
root_cause: Cluster‑autoscaler was unable to provision new nodes because the node‑pool had reached the maximum size allowed by the quota, leaving the HPA unable to scale up.
resolution: I increased the max nodes for the node‑pool in the autoscaler config from 10 to 20 (`kubectl edit hpa user-auth-hpa` and updated the autoscaler YAML). Then I triggered a manual scale‑up (`kubectl scale deployment user-auth --replicas=8`). The HPA now reports 8/8 and pods are running.

title: Order‑service HPA stuck at 3 replicas, users seeing timeout errors
description: The order‑service was only running 3 pods while the desired count was 12, causing 504 timeouts. `kubectl get hpa order-service-hpa -o yaml | grep -i desired` showed `desiredReplicas: 12` but `currentReplicas: 3`. Logs contained `HPA "order-service-hpa" cannot scale due to resource quota limits` and pods were evicted with priority `system-node-critical`.
root_cause: A recently added pod‑priority class caused the autoscaler to evict low‑priority pods, preventing the HPA from creating new replicas due to insufficient resource quota.
resolution: I lowered the priority class of the new pods to `user-critical` (`kubectl edit priorityclass high-priority-pods`) and updated the resource quota to allow 15 replicas (`kubectl edit quota default`). After restarting the deployment, the HPA scaled to 12 replicas and the timeouts disappeared.

title: notifications-worker job stalled over an hour
description: The notifications-worker batch job has been hanging for more than an hour. `kubectl -n prod describe job notifications-worker-20241013-01` shows the pod stuck in `Completed` with a `DeadlineExceeded` event: `Error: job failed after 1h: deadline exceeded`. The job logs contain `timeout error: context deadline exceeded`.
root_cause: The job container had a CPU limit that was too low, causing the process to be throttled and unable to finish within the default 1‑hour deadline.
resolution: Scaled the job's CPU request/limit from 100m to 500m, then restarted the job: `kubectl -n prod delete job notifications-worker-20241013-01 && kubectl -n prod apply -f notifications-worker-job.yaml`. The job completed in 15 minutes.

title: search-api job timing out during nightly data import
description: The nightly search-api data import job exceeds its 1h timeout. `kubectl -n prod describe job search-api-import-20241013` shows `Last probe failure: TimeoutError: operation timed out after 3600s`. In the pod logs I see `WARN: Query execution took 55 minutes, aborting after 1h`.
root_cause: The job was configured with a default `activeDeadlineSeconds` of 3600 but the underlying database query was slower due to increased index fragmentation.
resolution: Dropped the deadline by setting `activeDeadlineSeconds: 7200` in the job spec and added a pod affinity to schedule on nodes with more memory. Applied changes with `kubectl -n prod apply -f search-api-import-job.yaml`. The import now finishes in under 2 hours.

title: ETL job crashing on nightly run
description: The nightly ETL job in reporting-etl failed with a `panic: runtime error: index out of range` error. `kubectl -n reporting-etl describe jobs nightly-etl-20241013` shows the pod status as Failed and the events list the termination reason as `Error` with `ExitCode=139`.
root_cause: The job image was built with an older version of the Go runtime that caused a memory corruption when processing large CSV files.
resolution: Pulled a newer image (`reporting-etl:1.4.2`), updated the Deployment to use this tag, and redeployed the Job. Verified logs no longer contain the panic and the job completes successfully. Added a health check to re‑run the job if it exits with a non‑zero code.

title: Order service job stuck in BackOff after crash
description: The order-service batch job started but quickly entered a `BackOff` state. `kubectl -n order-service describe pod order-batch-20241013-5d6f9` shows `Error: Failed to connect to DB: dial tcp 10.0.0.5:5432: connect: connection refused`. The pod logs contain `sql: connection timeout` messages.
root_cause: The database pod was evicted due to insufficient memory, causing the connection pool in the job to fail.
resolution: Scaled the PostgreSQL StatefulSet to 2 replicas, restarted the evicted pod, and updated the order-service ConfigMap to point to the new replica set. Re‑started the job; it now completes without errors. Implemented a readiness probe to prevent future jobs from starting when DB is unavailable.

title: Kubelet cert expired, node stuck in NotReady state
description:
The monitoring stack flagged a node as NotReady after a kubelet restart. `kubectl get nodes` shows `STATUS NotReady` and the kubelet log contains `error: client certificate expired: 2024-09-01T12:00:00Z`.

This is blocking pod scheduling for the reporting‑etl service.
root_cause: The node's kubelet client certificate had expired due to the cluster certificate rotation not being applied to all nodes.
resolution: SSH into the worker node and replaced the kubelet cert by running `kubeadm init phase certs kubelet-client` followed by `systemctl restart kubelet`. After a brief pause, the node returned to Ready and pods were scheduled.

title: User‑auth service outage after kubelet cert rollover
description:
After the recent kubelet certificate rotation, user‑auth pods started crashing with `Error: failed to connect to apiserver: x509: certificate has expired`. `kubectl logs <pod>` shows `kubelet: client certificate expired`.

The service was down for 15 minutes.
root_cause: The kubelet client certs were rotated on the master nodes but the new certs were not propagated to the control plane components used by user‑auth.
resolution: Updated the kubelet client certs on the control plane by re-running `kubeadm alpha certs renew all`. Then restarted the API server and controller manager, and redeployed the user‑auth deployment with `kubectl rollout restart deployment/user-auth`.

title: Kubelet cert renewal failed on node-12, node unusable
description: The monitoring stack shows kubelet on node-12 crashing with "error: failed to renew client certificate: certificate expired". `kubectl get nodes -o wide` lists node-12 as NotReady for the past 20 minutes.
root_cause: The client certificate for kubelet on node-12 had expired due to an incorrect clock sync on the node during a recent reboot.
resolution: Updated the node's time via NTP, then ran `kubeadm certs renew --cert-dir /etc/kubernetes/pki kubelet` on the control plane and restarted kubelet: `systemctl restart kubelet`. The node returned to Ready state within 5 minutes.

title: web-frontend node stuck after kubelet cert error
description: web-frontend pod deployments keep failing with "kubelet: authentication failed: cert has expired". `kubectl describe pod web-frontend-5d8c7c9f6-abcde` shows kubelet not starting due to certificate renewal failure.
root_cause: The kubelet client certificate for the web-frontend node was revoked by an upstream CA update, causing kubelet to reject new requests.
resolution: Removed the stale certificate from `/etc/kubernetes/pki/kubelet-client-current.pem`, regenerated it with `kubeadm certs renew kubelet --cert-dir /etc/kubernetes/pki`, copied the new cert to the node, and restarted kubelet. Pods started normally.

title: Kubelets on 3 nodes unresponsive, order-service stuck
description: Order-service pods keep crashing, kubectl exec returns `error: unable to connect to the server: dial tcp 192.168.10.5:6443: i/o timeout`. Checking node status shows `Ready` flag missing on three nodes. `journalctl -u kubelet.service` logs show `Failed to connect to the API server` errors.
root_cause: A misconfigured firewall rule dropped all traffic from the monitoring stack to the kubelet ports on the affected nodes.
resolution: Updated the firewall rules to allow TCP 10250/10255 traffic from the monitoring stack CIDR. Restarted kubelet on each node (`systemctl restart kubelet`). Verified nodes returned to Ready state and order-service pods resumed.

title: Notifications-worker pods cannot log, kubelet unreachable
description: Notifications-worker logs show repeated `kubectl logs` failures: `Error from server (BadGateway): Bad Gateway`. `kubectl get nodes` shows several nodes in `NotReady`. The monitoring stack reports `KubeletDown` after 15 minutes.
root_cause: The kubelet service on affected nodes had crashed due to a corrupted config file after a recent update.
resolution: Replaced the corrupted kubelet config files with backups, then restarted kubelet (`systemctl restart kubelet`) on all impacted nodes. Confirmed node readiness and restored notifications-worker pod logs.

title: Kubelet lagging on reporting‑etl node
description: The reporting‑etl pod was stuck in "ContainerCreating" for over 10 minutes, kubectl logs showed "Failed to pull image" but the image existed. The pod status stuck at "ContainerCreating" and kubelet metrics spiked to 99th percentile of 75s.
root_cause: The node’s disk was full, causing kubelet to delay the pod lifecycle events.
resolution: Executed `df -h` on the node, cleared old logs and container images (`docker system prune -a`), then restarted kubelet (`systemctl restart kubelet`). The pod started normally.

title: web‑frontend pods stuck at CrashLoopBackOff
description: After a deployment, web‑frontend pods repeatedly crashed with the error "Failed to fetch API: 500 Internal Server Error". The kubelet duration metrics showed an outlier of 60s on the affected node.
root_cause: A sudden spike in memory usage caused kubelet to delay pod termination, leaving stale cgroup files and leading to CrashLoopBackOff.
resolution: Scaled down the replica count to 0, cleaned stale cgroup directories (`rm -rf /sys/fs/cgroup/memory/kubepods/...`), then scaled replicas back up and restarted kubelet. Pods stabilized.

title: search‑api pods stuck in ContainerCreating for >10m
description: The search‑api deployment shows a spike in ContainerCreating duration. `kubectl describe pod search-api-7c8d9b5b4-abcde` shows `ContainerCreating` with reason `Pulling` and logs contain `EIO: I/O error while reading from device`. The latency metrics are at 99th percentile 15s.
root_cause: The node storage was throttling IOPS, causing kubelet to wait for volume attach operations.
resolution: Cordoned and drained the affected node with `kubectl cordon <node>` and `kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data`. Then deleted the node from the cluster and allowed it to re‑join, restoring normal pod start times.

title: inventory-db pod start failures after 2am
description: inventory-db pods are failing to start: `kubectl get pods inventory-db-xxxx -o wide` shows `Pending` state with event `Failed to attach or mount volume with error: i/o timeout`. Logs from kubelet show `kubelet: I/O error while reading from device`. The latency spike was recorded at 12s on the node.
root_cause: The node’s underlying SSD was hitting IOPS limits due to a concurrent backup job.
resolution: Stopped the backup job, cordoned the node (`kubectl cordon <node>`), drained it (`kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets`), and after the node was drained, restarted the backup job. The inventory-db pods now start within 1–2 seconds.

title: Kubelet cert expired – inventory-db pods crashing
description: Inventory‑db pods keep reporting "Kubelet: failed to connect to apiserver: tls: certificate has expired". The pods are stuck in CrashLoopBackOff and the API logs show "tls: certificate has expired". kubectl get pods inventory-db-abc123 -o wide shows status CrashLoopBackOff.
root_cause: The kubelet server certificate on node node-01 expired after the 90‑day renewal window was missed.
resolution:
Renewed the kubelet cert on node-01 using kubeadm: 
1. ssh to node-01 and run `kubeadm certs renew kubelet-serving`. 
2. Restart kubelet with `systemctl restart kubelet`. 
3. Verified with `kubectl get nodes -o yaml | grep expiration` that the new cert is valid. Pods resumed normal operation.

title: User‑auth unable to join cluster – node cert issue
description: User‑auth service nodes are repeatedly reporting "Failed to connect to Kubelet: tls: expired certificate". The kubelet logs contain "TLS handshake failed: certificate has expired". kubectl describe node user-auth-node-01 shows status NotReady.
root_cause: The kubelet server certificate on user‑auth-node-01 was generated with an old expiration date due to a mis‑configured renewal cron.
resolution:
Regenerated the kubelet cert on user‑auth-node-01: 
1. `kubeadm init phase certs kubelet-serving` to create a new cert. 
2. Copy the new certs to /etc/kubernetes/pki and restart kubelet (`systemctl restart kubelet`). 
3. Confirm node status with `kubectl get nodes`. The node returned to Ready and user‑auth traffic resumed.

title: Kubelet cert renewal failed on node causing payments pods to crash
description: The payments-service pods started to crash with errors like "kubelet: failed to renew server certificate" and a `kubectl get pods -o wide` shows many pods in CrashLoopBackOff. Logs from the node show `Failed to renew certificate: failed to update token: x509: certificate has expired`
root_cause: The node's kubelet certificate expired because the cluster's cert rotation interval was set too long and the renewal script failed due to missing permissions on the cert manager secret
resolution: Updated the kubelet certificates on all affected nodes by running `kubeadm init phase upload-certs --upload-certs` and then restarted kubelet services with `systemctl restart kubelet`. Verified the new certs are active via `kubectl describe node <node> | grep TLS`

title: Inventory DB nodes stuck after kubelet cert renewal error
description: Inventory-db node logs show `kubelet: failed to renew server certificate` and the node shows `Ready` but the pod status is `NotReady`. `kubectl get nodes` reports the node as `NotReady` and the inventory service cannot connect to the database.
root_cause: The kubelet on the inventory-db worker node failed to renew its server certificate because the cert-manager pod was unavailable during the renewal window
resolution: Deleted the problematic node from the cluster with `kubectl delete node <node>` and recreated it by running `kubeadm join` with the correct join token. After node rejoin, the inventory-db pod started normally and connectivity was restored.

title: Search‑API pods saturating node, kubelet throttling requests
description: The monitoring stack flagged a high number of pending API calls from search‑api. `kubectl get pods --all-namespaces --field-selector spec.nodeName=node-3 | wc -l` returned 118 pods, and logs show `E0801 12:34:56.123456 kubelet.go:1235] Too many pods: 118, maxPods=110`. The node is stuck, new pods cannot start.
root_cause: The node was over‑provisioned with search‑api pods beyond the default 110 pod limit, exhausting the kubelet’s maxPods capacity.
resolution: Drained node-3 and migrated 8 search‑api pods to node-4 with `kubectl drain node-3 --ignore-daemonsets && kubectl delete pod -l app=search-api -n prod --all` and then uncordoned node-3. Updated the cluster autoscaler to add an extra worker node, and adjusted the kubelet config to `maxPods: 120` on node-3 to accommodate future growth.

title: Inventory‑DB node hitting pod cap, causing write timeouts
description: Clients reported write timeouts to inventory‑db; logs show `pvc-xyz: error: pod "db‑replica‑3" exceeded maxPods` and the monitoring stack indicated 112 pods on node-5. The node’s CRI was rejecting new container starts.
root_cause: An automated deployment of a new inventory‑db replica added a pod to node-5, pushing it past the 110‑pod limit.
resolution: Removed the newest replica from node-5, redeployed it to node-6, and increased the kubelet’s `maxPods` to 115 on node-5 via the KubeletConfiguration file.
